result.summary: The Muse closes Arethusa's account: Ceres sends Triptolemus in her dragon-drawn chariot to spread grain, and when King Lyncus of Scythia tries to murder him, Ceres turns Lyncus into a lynx. The Nymphs then award the contest to the Muses, and the defeated Pierides, who abuse them, are turned into chattering magpies.

scenes.title: Triptolemus and Lyncus
scenes.summary: Ceres sends Triptolemus across the world to sow grain. In Scythia King Lyncus, jealous of the gift, tries to stab him in his sleep and is turned into a lynx.
scenes.stakes: Triptolemus risks being murdered in his sleep by a jealous host, and his mission could fail.

scenes.title: The Pierides become magpies
scenes.summary: The Nymphs judge the Muses the winners. The defeated Pierides hurl abuse and threats, and are changed into magpies that keep their talkativeness.
scenes.stakes: The Pierides face punishment for insulting the Muses after losing the contest.

alias_notes.explanation: Mopsopian means Athenian, from the old Attic king Mopsopus; here it describes Triptolemus.
Emathia is a poetic name for Macedonia, where the Pierides came from.

analysis.text: Both stories punish those who reject or abuse a gift: Lyncus envies the gift of agriculture, and the Pierides insult their judges. Transformation fits the offence.
Triptolemus links Athens and the Eleusinian Mysteries to the spread of farming, and Scythia stands for the barbarian outsider in Greek and Roman eyes.

legacy.text: Triptolemus sending out grain was a favourite subject of Greek vase painting and Athenian civic myth, tied to the Eleusinian Mysteries.

fun_facts.text: The magpie ending ties into Ovid's habit of explaining animal traits through myth; the Pierides' chattering becomes the magpie's cry.

language_notes.text: The Tritonian citadel is Athens, the city of Minerva (Pallas), who was associated with Lake Triton. Triptolemus was an Athenian prince.
Scythia was the vaguely known region north of the Black Sea, which Greeks and Romans regarded as wild and uncivilized.
"Barbarian" here means a non-Greek, uncivilized foreigner, as the Scythians were considered; it is not simply an insult to his manners.
"Mopsopian" means Athenian, from Mopsopus, an early legendary king of Attica.
"Sacred drawers" means the sacred dragons that draw Ceres' chariot.
Helicon is the Muses' mountain in Boeotia, so "the Goddesses who inhabit Helicon" are the Muses.
"Emathian" means Macedonian; Ovid uses it for the Pierides, daughters of Pierus, here loosely linked with northern Greece.

context_notes.text: Ceres (the Greek Demeter) is goddess of grain and agriculture. She sends Triptolemus to teach farming after her daughter's return.
The narrator is a Muse retelling the contest with the Pierides to Minerva. Arethusa's story was her song's last part, and "the greatest of us" is Calliope.
Magpies were known for noisy chatter, so the transformation fits the Pierides' boastful, quarrelsome natures.

literary_notes.text: Lyncus tries to kill the giver of a gift to humanity out of envy, and his own name becomes his punishment, a lynx.
The Pierides smile and scorn the threats while the reader knows, from the Muses' power, that they are about to suffer transformation themselves.
The picture of arms flapping into wings while the birds hang in the air makes the metamorphosis vivid and a little comic.
Their old habit of noisy talk survives the change, so the new form expresses their original character.
